rows.source: Of things some are in our power, and others are not. In our power are opinion, movement towards a thing, desire, aversion, turning from a thing; and in a word, whatever are our acts. Not in our power are the body, property, reputation, offices (magisterial power), and in a word, whatever are not our own acts. And the things in our power are by nature free, not subject to restraint or hindrance; but the things not in our power are weak, slavish, subject to restraint, in the power of others. Remember then, that if you think the things which are by nature slavish to be free, and the things which are in the power of others to be your own, you will be hindered, you will lament, you will be disturbed, you will blame both gods and men; but if you think that only which is your own to be your own, and if you think that what is another’s, as it really is, belongs to another, no man will ever compel you, no man will hinder you, you will never blame any man, you will accuse no man, you will do nothing involuntarily (against your will), no man will harm you, you will have no enemy, for you will not suffer any harm.
rows.before: Some things are within our control, others are not. Within our control are our opinions, impulses, desires, and aversions — in short, whatever is our own doing. Outside our control are our body, reputation, possessions, and positions of power — in short, whatever is not our own doing. What is within our control is by nature free, unhindered, unobstructed. What is outside our control is weak, dependent, subject to obstruction — it belongs to others. Remember: if you mistake what belongs to others for your own, you will be frustrated, you will grieve, you will be in turmoil, blaming gods and men alike. But if you take as your own only what truly is your own, and recognise that what belongs to others belongs to others, no one will ever compel you or obstruct you. You will blame no one, accuse no one, do nothing against your will. You will have no enemies, and nothing can harm you.
rows.after: Some things are within our control, others are not. Within our control are our opinions, impulses, desires, and aversions—what we seek to avoid. In short, whatever is our own doing. Outside our control are our body, reputation, possessions, and positions of power — in short, whatever is not our own doing. What is within our control is by nature free, unhindered, unobstructed. What is outside our control is weak, dependent, subject to obstruction — it belongs to others. Remember: if you mistake what is dependent for what is free, or what belongs to others for your own, you will be frustrated, you will grieve, you will be in turmoil, blaming gods and men alike. But if you take as your own only what truly is your own, and recognise that what belongs to others belongs to others, no one will ever compel you or obstruct you. You will blame no one, accuse no one, do nothing against your will. You will have no enemies, and nothing can harm you.

rows.source: If then you desire (aim at) such great things remember that you must not (attempt to) lay hold of them with a small effort; but you must leave alone some things entirely, and postpone others for the present. But if you wish for these things also (such great things), and power (office) and wealth, perhaps you will not gain even these very things (power and wealth) because you aim also at those former things (such great things); certainly you will fail in those things through which alone happiness and freedom are secured. Straightway then practise saying to every harsh appearance: You are an appearance, and in no manner what you appear to be. Then examine it by the rules which you possess, and by this first and chiefly, whether it relates to the things which are in our power or to things which are not in our power; and if it relates to anything which is not in our power, be ready to say that it does not concern you.
rows.before: If you aim at such great things, remember you must not pursue them halfheartedly. Some things must be given up entirely, others set aside for now. But if you want both — inner freedom and worldly power and wealth — you may well get neither, because the pursuit of one undermines the other. You will certainly fail to secure the things through which alone happiness and freedom are possible. Practise saying to every difficult impression: "You are an impression, not the reality." Then test it above all by this rule: does it concern what is within my control, or what is not? If not, train yourself to say: "This is nothing to me."
rows.after: If you aim at such great things, remember that you cannot pursue them with a small effort. Some things must be given up entirely, and others set aside for now. But if you pursue this freedom alongside worldly power and wealth, you may fail to gain even the power and wealth because you are pursuing freedom too. You will certainly miss what alone can secure happiness and freedom. An impression is how something first appears to you. Practise saying at once to every disturbing impression: "You are only an impression, and not at all what you appear to be." Then examine it by the rules you possess, first and above all by asking whether it concerns something within our control or something outside it. If it concerns something outside our control, be ready to say: "This does not concern me."

rows.source: Remember that desire contains in it the profession (hope) of obtaining that which you desire; and the profession (hope) in aversion (turning from a thing) is that you will not fall into that which you attempt to avoid; and he who fails in his desire is unfortunate; and he who falls into that which he would avoid is unhappy. If then you attempt to avoid only the things contrary to nature which are within your power you will not be involved in any of the things which you would avoid. But if you attempt to avoid disease, or death, or poverty, you will be unhappy. Take away then aversion from all things which are not in our power, and transfer it to the things contrary to nature which are in our power. But destroy desire completely for the present. For if you desire anything which is not in our power, you must be unfortunate; but of the things in our power, and which it would be good to desire, nothing yet is before you. But employ only the power of moving towards an object and retiring from it; and these powers indeed only slightly and with exceptions and with remission.
rows.before: Desire carries within it the expectation of getting what you desire; aversion carries the expectation of avoiding what you turn from. Whoever fails to get what they desire is unfortunate; whoever falls into what they are trying to avoid is unhappy. So: if you try to avoid only what is unnatural among the things within your control, you will never encounter what you want to avoid. But if you try to avoid sickness, death, or poverty, you will be unhappy. Remove aversion from everything outside your control and redirect it toward what is genuinely harmful within your control. For now, set aside desire entirely. If you desire anything outside your control, you must meet with disappointment. The things worth desiring within your control are not yet before you. Use only gentle impulse toward and away from things, held loosely and tentatively.
rows.after: Remember: desire holds out the hope of obtaining what you desire, while aversion holds out the hope of avoiding what you try to escape. Whoever fails to get what they desire is unfortunate; whoever falls into what they try to avoid is unhappy. If you try to avoid only what is contrary to nature among the things within your control, you will not fall into anything you seek to avoid. But if you try to avoid illness, death, or poverty, you will be unhappy. Remove aversion, then, from everything outside your control, and direct it toward what is contrary to nature within your control. For the present, give up desire entirely. If you desire anything outside your control, you are bound to be unfortunate; and of the good things within your control, nothing is yet before you to desire. Use only your impulses to move toward or away from things, and use even these gently, with reservation, and without strain.

rows.source: In everything which pleases the soul, or supplies a want, or is loved, remember to add this to the (description, notion): What is the nature of each thing, beginning from the smallest? If you love an earthen vessel, say it is an earthen vessel which you love; for when it has been broken you will not be disturbed. If you are kissing your child or wife, say that it is a human being whom you are kissing, for when the wife or child dies you will not be disturbed.
rows.before: Whenever something pleases you, or meets a need, or that you love, remind yourself of its nature. Start with small things. If you love a clay cup, say to yourself: it is a clay cup that I love. When it breaks, you will not be disturbed. If you kiss your child or your wife, say: it is a human being I am kissing. When they die, you will not be disturbed.

If you love a clay cup, say to yourself: it is a clay cup that I love. When it breaks, you will not be disturbed. If you kiss your child or your wife, say: it is a human being I am kissing. When they die, you will not be disturbed.

rows.source: When you are going to take in hand any act remind yourself what kind of an act it is. If you are going to bathe, place before yourself what happens in the bath; some splashing the water, others pushing against one another, others abusing one another, and some stealing; and thus with more safety you will undertake the matter, if you say to yourself, I now intend to bathe, and to maintain my will in a manner conformable to nature. And so you will do in every act; for thus if any hindrance to bathing shall happen let this thought be ready. It was not this only that I intended, but I intended also to maintain my will in a way conformable to nature; but I shall not maintain it so if I am vexed at what happens.
rows.before: Before taking on any activity, picture what it involves. If you are going to the baths, picture what happens there — people splashing, jostling, arguing, stealing. Then you will go more safely if you say to yourself: I want to bathe, and I want to keep my will in accordance with nature. Do this with every activity. That way, if something gets in the way of your bathing, you can say: that was not all I intended — I also intended to keep my will in accordance with nature. And I will not do that by getting upset over what happens.
rows.after: Before taking on any activity, picture what it involves. If you are going to the baths, picture what happens there—people splashing, jostling, insulting one another, and stealing. Then you will undertake it more safely if you say to yourself: "I intend to bathe, and I also intend to keep my will in accordance with nature." Do this with every activity. That way, if something prevents you from bathing, you can say: "Bathing was not my only intention. I also intended to keep my will in accordance with nature, and I will not do that if I am upset by what happens."

rows.source: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things; for example, death is nothing terrible, for if it were it would have seemed so to Socrates; for the opinion about death that it is terrible, is the terrible thing. When then we are impeded, or disturbed, or grieved, let us never blame others, but ourselves—that is, our opinions. It is the act of an ill-instructed man to blame others for his own bad condition; it is the act of one who has begun to be instructed, to lay the blame on himself; and of one whose instruction is completed, neither to blame another, nor himself.
rows.before: People are not disturbed by events but by their opinions about events. Death, for instance, is nothing terrible — if it were, it would have seemed terrible to Socrates. What is terrible is the opinion that death is terrible. So whenever we are frustrated, troubled, or distressed, let us never blame others, but ourselves — meaning our own opinions. It is the sign of an untrained person to blame others for their troubles; of one beginning to learn, to blame themselves; of one whose learning is complete, to blame neither others nor themselves.

rows.source: Be not elated at any advantage (excellence) which belongs to another. If a horse when he is elated should say, I am beautiful, one might endure it. But when you are elated, and say, I have a beautiful horse, you must know that you are elated at having a good horse. What then is your own? The use of appearances. Consequently when in the use of appearances you are conformable to nature, then be elated, for then you will be elated at something good which is your own.
rows.before: Do not take pride in advantages that belong to someone else. If a horse could say proudly "I am beautiful," that would be tolerable. But when you say proudly "I have a beautiful horse," you should know that you are taking pride in something that belongs to the horse. What is actually yours? The use of your impressions. When you use your impressions in accordance with nature, then be proud — for then you are proud of something genuinely good, and genuinely yours.
rows.after: Do not take pride in advantages that belong to someone else. If a horse could say proudly "I am beautiful," that would be tolerable. But when you say proudly "I have a beautiful horse," you should know that you are taking pride in something that belongs to the horse. What is actually yours? How you judge and respond to your impressions. When you do this in accordance with nature, then be proud — for then you are proud of something genuinely good, and genuinely yours.

rows.source: As on a voyage when the vessel has reached a port, if you go out to get water it is an amusement by the way to pick up a shellfish or some bulb, but your thoughts ought to be directed to the ship, and you ought to be constantly watching if the captain should call, and then you must throw away all those things, that you may not be bound and pitched into the ship like sheep. So in life also, if there be given to you instead of a little bulb and a shell a wife and child, there will be nothing to prevent (you from taking them). But if the captain should call, run to the ship and leave all those things without regard to them. But if you are old, do not even go far from the ship, lest when you are called you make default.
rows.before: On a sea voyage, when the ship puts into port and you go ashore to fetch water, you might pick up a shellfish or a plant along the way — but keep your eyes on the ship. When the captain calls, leave everything and run back. That is how it is in life too. If instead of a shellfish you are given a wife and child, there is nothing wrong with that. But when the captain calls, leave even them without hesitation. And if you are old, don't wander far from the ship in the first place, lest you be left behind when the call comes.
rows.after: On a sea voyage, when the ship reaches a port and you go ashore for water, you may amuse yourself by picking up a shellfish or a plant bulb along the way. But keep your thoughts on the ship and watch constantly for the captain's call. When he calls, throw everything aside, so that you are not tied up and thrown aboard like sheep. Life is like this too. If you are given a wife and child instead of a little bulb and a shell, there is nothing to prevent you from accepting them. But when the captain calls, run to the ship and leave everything without a second thought. If you are old, do not even go far from the ship, or you may fail to return when called.

rows.source: On the occasion of every accident (event) that befalls you, remember to turn to yourself and inquire what power you have for turning it to use. If you see a fair man or a fair woman, you will find that the power to resist is temperance (continence). If labor (pain) be presented to you, you will find that it is endurance. If it be abusive words, you will find it to be patience. And if you have been thus formed to the (proper) habit, the appearances will not carry you along with them.
rows.before: When any event befalls you, turn to yourself and ask what capacity you have to meet it. If you see someone attractive, the resource available to you is self-restraint. If you face hardship, it is endurance. If you are insulted, it is patience. Once you have formed this habit, events will not sweep you away.
rows.after: Whenever an event befalls you, remember to turn to yourself and ask what capacity you have to make use of it. If you see an attractive man or woman, you will find in yourself the capacity for self-restraint. If you face hard work or pain, you will find endurance. If you face abusive words, you will find patience. Once you have formed this habit, impressions will not sweep you away.

rows.source: Never say about anything, I have lost it, but say I have restored it. Is your child dead? It has been restored. Is your wife dead? She has been restored. Has your estate been taken from you? Has not then this also been restored? But he who has taken it from me is a bad man. But what is it to you, by whose hands the giver demanded it back? So long as he may allow you, take care of it as a thing which belongs to another, as travellers do with their inn.

rows.source: If you intend to improve, throw away such thoughts as these: if I neglect my affairs, I shall not have the means of living: unless I chastise my slave, he will be bad. For it is better to die of hunger and so to be released from grief and fear than to live in abundance with perturbation; and it is better for your slave to be bad than for you to be unhappy. Begin then from little things. Is the oil spilled? Is a little wine stolen? Say on the occasion, at such price is sold freedom from perturbation; at such price is sold tranquillity, but nothing is got for nothing. And when you call your slave, consider that it is possible that he does not hear; and if he does hear, that he will do nothing which you wish. But matters are not so well with him, but altogether well with you, that it should be in his power for you to be not disturbed.
rows.before: If you are working to improve yourself, let go of thoughts like: "If I neglect my business I will have nothing to live on," or "If I don't discipline my servant he will become lazy." It is better to die of hunger free from grief and fear than to live in abundance troubled and anxious. And it is better for your servant to be lazy than for you to be miserable. Begin with small things. Oil spilled, wine stolen — say to yourself: this is the price of peace of mind; this is the price of tranquility. Nothing comes for free. When you call your servant, bear in mind that he may not hear, or hearing, may not do what you ask. He does not have the power to disturb you — but you have the power not to be disturbed.
rows.after: If you are working to improve yourself, let go of thoughts like: "If I neglect my affairs, I will have nothing to live on," or "Unless I discipline my slave, he will behave badly." It is better to die of hunger free from grief and fear than to live in abundance troubled and anxious. And it is better for your slave to behave badly than for you to be unhappy. Begin with small things. Has some oil been spilled? Has a little wine been stolen? Say: "This is the price of freedom from distress; this is the price of peace of mind. Nothing comes for nothing." When you call your slave, bear in mind that he may not hear; and if he does hear, he may do nothing you want. He is not the one in such a fortunate position; you are. Your freedom from distress must not lie in his power.

rows.source: If you would improve, submit to be considered without sense and foolish with respect to externals. Wish to be considered to know nothing; and if you shall seem to some to be a person of importance, distrust yourself. For you should know that it is not easy both to keep your will in a condition conformable to nature and (to secure) external things: but if a man is careful about the one, it is an absolute necessity that he will neglect the other.

rows.source: If you would have your children and your wife and your friends to live for ever, you are silly; for you would have the things which are not in your power to be in your power, and the things which belong to others to be yours. So if you would have your slave to be free from faults, you are a fool; for you would have badness not to be badness, but something else. But if you wish not to fail in your desires, you are able to do that. Practise then this which you are able to do. He is the master of every man who has the power over the things which another person wishes or does not wish, the power to confer them on him or to take them away. Whoever then wishes to be free let him neither wish for anything nor avoid anything which depends on others: if he does not observe this rule, he must be a slave.
rows.before: To wish your children, wife, and friends to live forever is foolish — you are wishing for things outside your control to be in your control, for what belongs to others to be yours. Equally, if you wish your servant to make no mistakes, you are wishing that what is bad were not bad. But if you want to succeed in your desires, that is something you can actually do. Practise what is in your power. The master of any person is whoever controls what that person wants or doesn't want — whoever can grant it or withhold it. Anyone who wants to be free must want nothing and avoid nothing that lies in another's power. Otherwise they are a slave.
rows.after: To wish your children, wife, and friends to live forever is foolish: you are wishing for things outside your control to be in your control, and for what belongs to others to be yours. Likewise, if you wish your slave to be free from faults, you are foolish; you are wishing badness not to be badness, but something else. But if you wish not to fail in your desires, that is within your power. Practise, then, what you are able to do. Anyone who controls the things another person wants or seeks to avoid—who can grant or take them away—is that person's master. Whoever wants to be free must neither desire nor avoid anything that depends on others. Otherwise, that person must be a slave.

rows.source: Remember that in life you ought to behave as at a banquet. Suppose that something is carried round and is opposite to you. Stretch out your hand and take a portion with decency. Suppose that it passes by you. Do not detain it. Suppose that it is not yet come to you. Do not send your desire forward to it, but wait till it is opposite to you. Do so with respect to children, so with respect to a wife, so with respect to magisterial offices, so with respect to wealth, and you will be some time a worthy partner of the banquets of the gods. But if you take none of the things which are set before you, and even despise them, then you will be not only a fellow banqueter with the gods, but also a partner with them in power. For by acting thus Diogenes and Heracleitus and those like them were deservedly divine, and were so called.
rows.before: At a banquet, remember to behave like a proper guest. When a dish is passed to you, reach out and take your portion gracefully. When it passes by, don't hold it back. When it hasn't reached you yet, don't reach forward — wait until it comes to you. Do this with children, with a spouse, with public office, with wealth, and you will prove a worthy guest at the gods' own table. But if you don't even take what is offered, if you actually refuse it — then you will share not just the gods' banquet but their power. This is how Diogenes and Heraclitus and those like them earned the name divine.
rows.after: Remember to behave in life as you would at a banquet. When a dish is passed to you, reach out and take your portion gracefully. When it passes by, don't hold it back. When it hasn't reached you yet, do not long for it ahead of time—wait until it comes to you. Do this with children, with a spouse, with public office, with wealth, and you will prove a worthy guest at the gods' own table. But if you don't even take what is offered, and even look down on it — then you will share not just the gods' banquet but their power. This is how Diogenes and Heraclitus and those like them deserved to be called divine, and were.

rows.source: When you see a person weeping in sorrow either when a child goes abroad or when he is dead, or when the man has lost his property, take care that the appearance do not hurry you away with it, as if he were suffering in external things. But straightway make a distinction in your own mind, and be in readiness to say, it is not that which has happened that afflicts this man, for it does not afflict another, but it is the opinion about this thing which afflicts the man. So far as words then do not be unwilling to show him sympathy, and even if it happens so, to lament with him. But take care that you do not lament internally also.
rows.before: When you see someone weeping in grief — because a child has gone away, or died, or because they have lost property — be careful not to be carried away by the appearance that they are suffering from external events. Draw a distinction in your own mind and be ready to say: what distresses this person is not what has happened — the same thing would not distress someone else — but their opinion about what has happened. In your words, by all means sympathise with them and even share their grief if the moment calls for it. But do not grieve inside as well.

rows.source: Remember that thou art an actor in a play, of such a kind as the teacher (author) may choose; if short, of a short one; if long, of a long one: if he wishes you to act the part of a poor man, see that you act the part naturally; if the part of a lame man, of a magistrate, of a private person, (do the same). For this is your duty, to act well the part that is given to you; but to select the part, belongs to another.
rows.before: Remember that you are an actor in a play whose length is determined by the author. If he wants it short, it is short; if long, long. If he wants you to play a poor man, play that role naturally; if a cripple, a magistrate, an ordinary person — do the same. Your duty is to act well the part you have been given. But choosing the part belongs to someone else.

rows.source: Let not these thoughts afflict you, I shall live unhonored and be nobody nowhere. For if want of honor is an evil, you cannot be in evil through the means (fault) of another any more than you can be involved in anything base. Is it then your business to obtain the rank of a magistrate, or to be received at a banquet? By no means. How then can this be want of honor (dishonor)? And how will you be nobody nowhere, when you ought to be somebody in those things only which are in your power, in which indeed it is permitted to you to be a man of the greatest worth? But your friends will be without assistance! What do you mean by being without assistance? They will not receive money from you, nor will you make them Roman citizens. Who then told you that these are among the things which are in our power, and not in the power of others? And who can give to another what he has not himself? Acquire money then, your friends say, that we also may have something. If I can acquire money and also keep myself modest and faithful and magnanimous, point out the way, and I will acquire it. But if you ask me to lose the things which are good and my own, in order that you may gain the things which are not good, see how unfair and silly you are. Besides, which would you rather have, money or a faithful and modest friend? For this end then rather help me to be such a man, and do not ask me to do this by which I shall lose that character. But my country, you say, as far as it depends on me, will be without my help. I ask again, what help do you mean? It will not have porticos or baths through you. And what does this mean? For it is not furnished with shoes by means of a smith, nor with arms by means of a shoemaker. But it is enough if every man fully discharges the work that is his own: and if you provided it with another citizen faithful and modest, would you not be useful to it? Yes. Then you also cannot be useless to it. What place then, you say, shall I hold in the city? Whatever you can, if you maintain at the same time your fidelity and modesty. But if when you wish to be useful to the state, you shall lose these qualities, what profit could you be to it, if you were made shameless and faithless?

rows.source: Has any man been preferred before you at a banquet, or in being saluted, or in being invited to a consultation? If these things are good, you ought to rejoice that he has obtained them; but if bad, be not grieved because you have not obtained them. And remember that you cannot, if you do not the same things in order to obtain what is not in our own power, be considered worthy of the same (equal) things. For how can a man obtain an equal share with another when he does not visit a man’s doors as that other man does; when he does not attend him when he goes abroad, as the other man does; when he does not praise (flatter) him as another does? You will be unjust then and insatiable, if you do not part with the price, in return for which those things are sold, and if you wish to obtain them for nothing. Well, what is the price of lettuces? An obolus perhaps. If then a man gives up the obolus, and receives the lettuces, and if you do not give up the obolus and do not obtain the lettuces, do not suppose that you receive less than he who has got the lettuces; for as he has the lettuces, so you have the obolus which you did not give. In the same way then in the other matter also you have not been invited to a man’s feast, for you did not give to the host the price at which the supper is sold; but he sells it for praise (flattery), he sells it for personal attention. Give then the price, if it is for your interest, for which it is sold. But if you wish both not to give the price and to obtain the things, you are insatiable and silly. Have you nothing then in place of the supper? You have indeed, you have the not flattering of him, whom you did not choose to flatter; you have the not enduring of the man when he enters the room.
rows.before: Was someone else given a higher place at a banquet, or greeted more warmly, or consulted first? If these things are good, be glad they got them; if bad, don't be troubled that you didn't. And remember: if you don't do what others do to obtain things outside your power, you cannot claim an equal share. How can you expect to be treated like someone who flatters and attends and praises the host, when you yourself do none of that? It would be unfair and unreasonable to want the goods without paying the price. What is the price of a head of lettuce? One coin, perhaps. If someone pays the coin, they get the lettuce. If you don't pay, you don't get it. But don't think you've come away with less than the person who has the lettuce — you still have the coin you didn't pay. In the same way, you weren't invited to someone's dinner: you didn't pay the price the host charges, which is flattery and personal attention. If you think it's worth paying, then pay it. But if you want both — to keep your self-respect and to have the dinner — you are being greedy and foolish. What do you have instead of the dinner? You have the fact of not having flattered the person you chose not to flatter. You have not having to endure their company.

Pay that price, if doing so is in your interest. But if you want both to avoid paying and to receive the goods, you are insatiable and foolish. Have you received nothing in place of the dinner? You have: you did not flatter the person you chose not to flatter, and you did not have to endure him when he entered the room.

rows.source: We may learn the wish (will) of nature from the things in which we do not differ from one another: for instance, when your neighbor’s slave has broken his cup, or anything else, we are ready to say forthwith, that it is one of the things which happen. You must know then that when your cup also is broken, you ought to think as you did when your neighbor’s cup was broken. Transfer this reflection to greater things also. Is another man’s child or wife dead? There is no one who would not say, This is an event incident to man. But when a man’s own child or wife is dead, forthwith he calls out, Woe to me, how wretched I am! But we ought to remember how we feel when we hear that it has happened to others.

rows.source: In every act observe the things which come first, and those which follow it; and so proceed to the act. If you do not, at first you will approach it with alacrity, without having thought of the things which will follow; but afterwards, when certain base (ugly) things have shown themselves, you will be ashamed. A man wishes to conquer at the Olympic games. I also wish indeed, for it is a fine thing. But observe both the things which come first, and the things which follow; and then begin the act. You must do everything according to rule, eat according to strict orders, abstain from delicacies, exercise yourself as you are bid at appointed times, in heat, in cold, you must not drink cold water, nor wine as you choose; in a word, you must deliver yourself up to the exercise master as you do to the physician, and then proceed to the contest. And sometimes you will strain the hand, put the ankle out of joint, swallow much dust, sometimes be flogged, and after all this be defeated. When you have considered all this, if you still choose, go to the contest: if you do not you will behave like children, who at one time play at wrestlers, another time as flute players, again as gladiators, then as trumpeters, then as tragic actors. So you also will be at one time an athlete, at another a gladiator, then a rhetorician, then a philosopher, but with your whole soul you will be nothing at all; but like an ape you imitate everything that you see, and one thing after another pleases you. For you have not undertaken anything with consideration, nor have you surveyed it well; but carelessly and with cold desire. Thus some who have seen a philosopher and having heard one speak, as Euphrates speaks—and who can speak as he does?—they wish to be philosophers themselves also. My man, first of all consider what kind of thing it is; and then examine your own nature, if you are able to sustain the character. Do you wish to be a pentathlete or a wrestler? Look at your arms, your thighs, examine your loins. For different men are formed by nature for different things. Do you think that if you do these things, you can eat in the same manner, drink in the same manner, and in the same manner loathe certain things? You must pass sleepless nights, endure toil, go away from your kinsmen, be despised by a slave, in everything have the inferior part, in honor, in office, in the courts of justice, in every little matter. Consider these things, if you would exchange for them, freedom from passions, liberty, tranquillity. If not, take care that, like little children, you be not now a philosopher, then a servant of the publicani, then a rhetorician, then a procurator (manager) for Cæsar. These things are not consistent. You must be one man, either good or bad. You must either cultivate your own ruling faculty, or external things. You must either exercise your skill on internal things or on external things; that is you must either maintain the position of a philosopher or that of a common person.

If you don't, you will begin with enthusiasm, not having thought through the consequences, and then feel ashamed when difficulties appear. A man wants to win at the Olympic games. You must live by strict routine, eat under orders, avoid sweets, train at set times in heat and cold, drink no cold water, drink no wine except as prescribed — in short, surrender yourself to the trainer as you would to a doctor. Then in the contest itself, you may sprain a wrist, twist an ankle, swallow a mouthful of sand, be flogged — and after all that, be beaten. Consider all this first. If you still want to go ahead, then go. Otherwise you will behave like a child who plays at being a wrestler one minute, a gladiator the next, then a trumpeter, then an actor — you too will be an athlete today, a philosopher tomorrow, an orator the day after, nothing with your whole soul. Like a monkey, you imitate whatever you see, and each new thing catches your fancy before you have considered whether it suits you. Someone sees a philosopher and hears him speak well, and immediately wants to become a philosopher too. My friend, first consider what kind of thing philosophy is. You will have to stay up at night, endure hardship, leave your family, be looked down on by a servant, be last in everything — in status, in honor, in the courts. Consider whether you are willing to trade all this for freedom from passion, for liberty, for tranquility. If not, don't become a philosopher — don't be like the child who is a philosopher today and a tax collector tomorrow. Choose one thing. You are either a good person or not. rows.source: Duties are universally measured by relations. Is a man a father? The precept is to take care of him, to yield to him in all things, to submit when he is reproachful, when he inflicts blows. But suppose that he is a bad father. Were you then by nature made akin to a good father? No; but to a father. Does a brother wrong you? Maintain then your own position towards him, and do not examine what he is doing, but what you must do that your will shall be conformable to nature. For another will not damage you, unless you choose: but you will be damaged then when you shall think that you are damaged. In this way then you will discover your duty from the relation of a neighbor, from that of a citizen, from that of a general, if you are accustomed to contemplate the relations.

rows.source: As to piety towards the gods you must know that this is the chief thing, to have right opinions about them, to think that they exist, and that they administer the All well and justly; and you must fix yourself in this principle (duty), to obey them, and to yield to them in everything which happens, and voluntarily to follow it as being accomplished by the wisest intelligence. For if you do so, you will never either blame the gods, nor will you accuse them of neglecting you. And it is not possible for this to be done in any other way than by withdrawing from the things which are not in our power, and by placing the good and the evil only in those things which are in our power. If your brother acts unjustly, do not lay hold of the act by that handle wherein he acts unjustly, for this is the handle which cannot be borne; but lay hold of the other, that he is your brother, that he was nurtured with you, and you will lay hold of the thing by that handle by which it can be borne.

rows.source: On no occasion call yourself a philosopher, and do not speak much among the uninstructed about theorems (philosophical rules, precepts); but do that which follows from them. For example, at a banquet do not say how a man ought to eat, but eat as you ought to eat. For remember that in this way Socrates also altogether avoided ostentation. Persons used to come to him and ask to be recommended by him to philosophers, and he used to take them to philosophers, so easily did he submit to being overlooked. Accordingly, if any conversation should arise among uninstructed persons about any theorem, generally be silent; for there is great danger that you will immediately vomit up what you have not digested. And when a man shall say to you that you know nothing, and you are not vexed, then be sure that you have begun the work (of philosophy). For even sheep do not vomit up their grass and show to the shepherds how much they have eaten; but when they have internally digested the pasture, they produce externally wool and milk. Do you also show not your theorems to the uninstructed, but show the acts which come from their digestion.
rows.before: Never call yourself a philosopher, and don't talk at length to uninstructed people about philosophical arguments. Show what you have learned through action. At a dinner party, don't lecture people about how one ought to eat — eat as one ought. Remember how completely Socrates avoided showing off. People would come to him and ask to be introduced to philosophers, and he would take them along — so readily did he keep himself in the background. If a philosophical topic comes up among uninstructed people, generally stay silent — it is very easy to start talking before you have properly digested what you know. When someone tells you that you know nothing and you are not stung by it, that is when you know you have actually begun philosophy. Even sheep don't regurgitate their grass to show the shepherd how much they have eaten — they digest it and produce wool and milk. Don't display your principles to the uninstructed. Display the conduct that comes from digesting them.

At a banquet, for example, do not explain how people ought to eat; eat as you ought. Remember how completely Socrates avoided showing off. People would come to him and ask him to recommend philosophers, and he would take them to philosophers, so readily did he accept being overlooked. If a conversation about a philosophical principle arises among people untrained in philosophy, generally stay silent. There is a great danger that you will immediately vomit up what you have not digested. When someone tells you that you know nothing and you are not upset, be sure that you have begun the work of philosophy. Even sheep do not vomit up their grass to show the shepherds how much they have eaten. They digest their food within and produce wool and milk outside. In the same way, do not display your principles to people untrained in philosophy. Show the actions that come from digesting them.

rows.source: When at a small cost you are supplied with everything for the body, do not be proud of this; nor, if you drink water, say on every occasion, I drink water. But consider first how much more frugal the poor are than we, and how much more enduring of labor. And if you ever wish to exercise yourself in labor and endurance, do it for yourself, and not for others. Do not embrace statues; but if you are ever very thirsty, take a draught of cold water and spit it out, and tell no man.

rows.source: The condition and characteristic of an uninstructed person is this: he never expects from himself profit (advantage) nor harm, but from externals. The condition and characteristic of a philosopher is this: he expects all advantage and all harm from himself. The signs (marks) of one who is making progress are these: he censures no man, he praises no man, he blames no man, he accuses no man, he says nothing about himself as if he were somebody or knew something; when he is impeded at all or hindered, he blames himself; if a man praises him he ridicules the praiser to himself; if a man censures him he makes no defence; he goes about like weak persons, being careful not to move any of the things which are placed, before they are firmly fixed; he removes all desire from himself, and he transfers aversion to those things only of the things within our power which are contrary to nature; he employs a moderate movement towards everything; whether he is considered foolish or ignorant he cares not; and in a word he watches himself as if he were an enemy and lying in ambush.
rows.before: The condition of an uninstructed person is this: they expect all their benefit and all their harm to come from externals. The condition of a philosopher is this: they expect all benefit and all harm from themselves. The signs of someone making progress: they blame no one, they praise no one, they complain about no one, they accuse no one, they say nothing about themselves as if they were important or knew something. When they are hindered or frustrated, they blame themselves. If someone praises them, they laugh at the praise to themselves. If someone censures them, they make no defence. They move carefully, like a convalescent, so as not to disturb anything before it has properly healed. They have cleared out all desire. They have redirected aversion to only those things within their control that are genuinely contrary to nature. Their impulses are moderate throughout. Whether they seem foolish or ignorant, they don't care. In a word, they watch themselves as if they were an enemy lying in wait.
rows.after: Someone untrained in philosophy never expects benefit or harm to come from themselves, but from things outside them. A philosopher expects all benefit and harm to come from themselves. These are the signs of someone making progress: they criticise no one, praise no one, blame no one, and accuse no one. They say nothing about themselves as though they were important or knew something. When obstructed or hindered, they blame themselves. If someone praises them, they privately laugh at the person praising them; if someone criticises them, they make no defence. They move about like someone physically weak, careful not to disturb anything that has been put in place before it is firmly settled. They set aside all desire and direct aversion only towards what is contrary to nature among the things within our control. Their impulses towards everything are moderate. They do not care whether others consider them foolish or ignorant. In short, they watch themselves as though they were an enemy lying in ambush.

rows.source: When a man is proud because he can understand and explain the writings of Chrysippus, say to yourself, If Chrysippus had not written obscurely, this man would have had nothing to be proud of. But what is it that I wish? To understand nature and to follow it. I inquire therefore who is the interpreter? and when I have heard that it is Chrysippus, I come to him (the interpreter). But I do not understand what is written, and therefore I seek the interpreter. And so far there is yet nothing to be proud of. But when I shall have found the interpreter, the thing that remains is to use the precepts (the lessons). This itself is the only thing to be proud of. But if I shall admire the exposition, what else have I been made unless a grammarian instead of a philosopher? except in one thing, that I am explaining Chrysippus instead of Homer. When, then, any man says to me, Read Chrysippus to me, I rather blush, when I cannot show my acts like to and consistent with his words.

If instead I just admire the explanation, I have become a literary critic, not a philosopher — except that I am analysing Chrysippus instead of Homer. When someone asks me to read Chrysippus to them, I feel ashamed when I cannot point to conduct that matches what I have read.

But I do not understand what he has written, so I seek someone to explain it. So far there is nothing to be proud of. Once I have found an interpreter, what remains is to put the lessons into practice. That alone is something to be proud of. If I merely admire the explanation, what have I become but a scholar of texts instead of a philosopher? The only difference is that I explain Chrysippus rather than Homer. rows.source: Whatever things (rules) are proposed to you (for the conduct of life) abide by them, as if they were laws, as if you would be guilty of impiety if you transgressed any of them. And whatever any man shall say about you, do not attend to it; for this is no affair of yours. How long will you then still defer thinking yourself worthy of the best things, and in no matter transgressing the distinctive reason? Have you accepted the theorems (rules), which it was your duty to agree to, and have you agreed to them? what teacher then do you still expect that you defer to him the correction of yourself? You are no longer a youth, but already a full-grown man. If, then, you are negligent and slothful, and are continually making procrastination after procrastination, and proposal (intention) after proposal, and fixing day after day, after which you will attend to yourself, you will not know that you are not making improvement, but you will continue ignorant (uninstructed) both while you live and till you die. Immediately then think it right to live as a full-grown man, and one who is making proficiency, and let everything which appears to you to be the best be to you a law which must not be transgressed. And if anything laborious or pleasant or glorious or inglorious be presented to you, remember that now is the contest, now are the Olympic games, and they cannot be deferred; and that it depends on one defeat and one giving way that progress is either lost or maintained. Socrates in this way became perfect, in all things improving himself, attending to nothing except to reason. But you, though you are not yet a Socrates, ought to live as one who wishes to be a Socrates.
rows.before: Whatever principles you have decided on for your conduct, hold to them as if they were laws — as if you would be breaking a sacred duty to violate them. Whatever anyone says about you, do not be concerned with it. This is none of your business. How long will you keep putting off the decision to be worthy of the best things, and to obey the reason that distinguishes you in every particular? You have accepted the principles you were meant to accept. What further teacher are you waiting for? You are no longer a boy. You are a grown person. If you go on being negligent and lazy, always postponing, making plan after plan, setting day after day after which you will finally pay attention to yourself — you will die without having improved, and you will never even know it. Start now: decide to live as an adult, as someone making real progress. Let what you truly believe to be best be a law you never break. If something hard or pleasant or glorious or inglorious is placed before you, the contest is now. The Olympic games are not deferred. A single defeat, a single surrender, and the progress already made is either lost or secured. This is how Socrates became what he was — improving in everything, attending to nothing but reason. Even if you are not yet Socrates, you ought to live like someone who wants to be.
rows.after: Hold to the rules laid down for your conduct as if they were laws, and breaking any of them would violate a sacred duty. Pay no attention to what anyone says about you; it is not your concern. How much longer will you wait before considering yourself worthy of the best things and resolving never to act against the power of reason that distinguishes you? Have you accepted the principles you ought to accept, and agreed to them? What teacher are you still waiting for, leaving your own correction until they arrive? You are no longer a youth but a grown adult. If you remain careless and lazy, postponing again and again, making plan after plan and setting date after date to begin attending to yourself, you will not notice that you are making no progress. You will remain untrained throughout your life and at your death. Decide now to live as a grown adult who is making progress. Treat whatever seems best to you as a law you must not break. If anything hard or pleasant, glorious or shameful, comes your way, remember: the contest is now, the Olympic Games are now, and they cannot be postponed. A single defeat, a single surrender, determines whether your progress is lost or maintained. This is how Socrates became perfect: improving himself in everything and attending to nothing but reason. Though you are not yet Socrates, live as someone who wishes to be like him.

rows.source: The first and most necessary place (part, ) in philosophy is the use of theorems (precepts, ), for instance, that we must not lie; the second part is that of demonstrations, for instance, How is it proved that we ought not to lie? The third is that which is confirmatory of these two, and explanatory, for example, How is this a demonstration? For what is demonstration, what is consequence, what is contradiction, what is truth, what is falsehood? The third part (topic) is necessary on account of the second, and the second on account of the first; but the most necessary and that on which we ought to rest is the first. But we do the contrary. For we spend our time on the third topic, and all our earnestness is about it; but we entirely neglect the first. Therefore we lie; but the demonstration that we ought not to lie we have ready to hand.

The second part is providing demonstrations: how do we know you must not lie? The third part is securing and explaining those demonstrations: what is a demonstration? What is entailment? What is contradiction? What is truth, what is falsehood? The third part is needed to support the second, and the second to support the first. But the first is the most important — the one we should rest in. We do the opposite. We spend all our time on the third part, applying all our enthusiasm to it, while entirely neglecting the first. So we lie — but we have the demonstration that we ought not to lie readily to hand.

But the first is the most necessary, and the one we should concentrate on. We do the opposite. We spend our time and all our effort on the third part, while entirely neglecting the first. So we lie, but have the proof that we ought not to lie ready to hand.
